claim: Participant NS is a tetraplegic adult with a C3-C4 spinal cord injury sustained approximately 10 years before the study.
source: The study participant NS has an AIS-A spinal cord injury at cervical level C3–C4 that she sustained approximately 10 years before this study.
evidence: Directly stated in the Materials and methods section describing the study participant.

claim: Participant NS was implanted with two 96-channel Neuroport Utah electrode arrays in the left posterior parietal cortex at the junction of the postcentral and intraparietal sulci.
source: As part of a BCI clinical study (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT01958086), participant NS was implanted with two 96-channel Neuroport Utah electrode arrays (Blackrock Microsystems model numbers 4382 and 4383).
evidence: Directly stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Participant NS achieved 86% overall accuracy in online BCI finger control across 10 sessions.
source: High classification accuracy during online control (86% ± SD 4% over 10 sessions; chance = 17%) (Figure 1b and Figure 1—figure supplement 3) and offline cross-validated classification (92% ± SD 2%; Figure 1—figure supplement 4a) demonstrated that the finger representations were reliable and linearly separable.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing classification accuracy across multiple sessions, with reference to Figure 1b showing the confusion matrix.

claim: 89% of recorded neurons were significantly tuned to individual finger-press movements.
source: At the single-neuron level, most (89%) neurons were significantly tuned to individual finger-press movements (significance threshold: p < 0.05, FDR-corrected) (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of single-neuron tuning data.

claim: The finger representational structure in participant NS matched the able-bodied fMRI model significantly better than the unstructured model.
source: The measured representational structure matched the able-bodied representational structure significantly over the unstructured model (p = 5.7 × 10–5, two-tailed t-test) (Figure 2f), ruling out the despecialization hypothesis (2).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison using whitened unbiased cosine similarity (WUC) metric.

claim: Participant NS's finger representational structure was consistent across multiple recording sessions.
source: Indeed, participant NS's finger RDMs were largely consistent across different recording sessions (average pairwise correlation, excluding the diagonal: r = 0.90 ± SD 0.04, min 0.83, max 0.99).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis of RDMs across sessions.

claim: The representational structure did not trend toward the task-optimal unstructured model over time.
source: However, we did not find conclusive evidence for a trend from the able-bodied model toward the unstructured model (linear-model session × model interaction: t(6) = 0.50, one-tailed t-test p = 0.32, Bayes factor [BF] = 0.66) (Figure 3a).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis showing no significant trend over sessions.

claim: The majority (70%) of online classification errors were middle-ring or ring-pinky confusions.
source: The majority (70%) of the online classification errors were middle-ring or ring-pinky confusions (Figure 1b).
evidence: Supported by analysis of the confusion matrix from online BCI control.

claim: The middle-ring and ring-pinky inter-finger distances did not increase over the course of the experiment despite systematic classification errors.
source: Contrary to this prediction, the middle-ring and ring-pinky distances did not increase over the course of the experiment (across sessions: t(8) = −4.5, one-tailed t-test p > 0.99, BF = 0.03; across runs within sessions: t(82) = −0.45, one-tailed t-test p = 0.67, BF = 0.12) (Figure 3b).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of inter-finger distances over time.

claim: Neural activity during finger movements exhibited a dynamic representational structure, with the muscle model emerging 170 ms earlier than the somatotopy model.
source: Figure 4e shows the decomposition of the representational structure into the muscle and somatotopy component models. The results show a dynamic structure, with the muscle model emerging 170 ms earlier than the somatotopy model (p = 0.002, two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
evidence: Supported by time-resolved representational similarity analysis showing temporal dynamics.

claim: The 170 ms timing difference between muscle and somatotopy models was consistent across individual sessions.
source: This timing difference was consistent across individual sessions (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) and task contexts, such as the calibration task (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by analysis across multiple sessions and task contexts.

claim: Participant NS's BCI control accuracy exceeded the previous best of other five-finger, online BCI control studies.
source: Her BCI control accuracy exceeded the previous best of other five-finger, online BCI control studies (Hotson et al., 2016; Jorge et al., 2020).
evidence: Comparison with previously published BCI studies.

claim: PC-IP is a candidate implant region for dexterous neural prostheses.
source: These results establish PC-IP as a candidate implant region for dexterous neural prostheses.
evidence: Inference drawn from the successful BCI control demonstrated in the study.

claim: This work is the first to discover individual finger representations in PPC.
source: Although previous studies have shown that the anterior intraparietal (AIP) area of PPC is involved in whole-hand grasping (Schaffelhofer and Scherberger, 2016; Klaes et al., 2015; Murata et al., 2000), our work is the first to discover individual finger representations in PPC (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Comparison with previous literature and presentation of novel findings.

claim: Participant NS's finger RDMs more strongly matched the able-bodied MC fMRI model than the PC-IP fMRI model.
source: Interestingly, participant NS's finger RDMs more strongly matched the able-bodied MC fMRI model, reaching similarities close to the theoretical maximum (Figure 2—figure supplement 3 and Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Supported by representational similarity analysis comparing different brain regions.

claim: The match between PC-IP spiking output and MC fMRI signals could suggest that PC-IP sends signals to MC, thereby driving the observed MC fMRI structure.
source: Thus, the match between PC-IP spiking output and MC fMRI signals could also suggest that PC-IP sends signals to MC, thereby driving the observed MC fMRI structure.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the observed match between PC-IP and MC representations.

claim: Motor representations in PPC reflect able-bodied motor usage patterns even after paralysis.
source: Our results reveal that motor representations in PPC reflect able-bodied motor usage patterns even after paralysis, and BCIs can re-engage these stable representations to restore lost motor functions.
evidence: Summary conclusion drawn from multiple analyses showing match with able-bodied patterns.

claim: BCIs can re-engage stable motor representations to restore lost motor functions.
source: Our results reveal that motor representations in PPC reflect able-bodied motor usage patterns even after paralysis, and BCIs can re-engage these stable representations to restore lost motor functions.
evidence: Inference drawn from successful BCI control using preserved representations.

claim: Participant NS cannot move or feel her hands due to her spinal cord injury.
source: Participant NS cannot move or feel her hands.
evidence: Direct statement about the participant's condition.

claim: The recording array was implanted at Talairach coordinates [−36 lateral, 48 posterior, 53 superior].
source: The recording array was implanted over the hand/limb region of the left PPC at the junction of the intraparietal sulcus with the postcentral sulcus (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Talairach coordinates [−36 lateral, 48 posterior, 53 superior]).
evidence: Specific anatomical coordinates provided for the implant location.

claim: Data were collected on 9 days over 6 weeks.
source: The data were collected on 9 days over 6 weeks.
evidence: Direct statement about the data collection timeline.

claim: Participant NS performed a reaction-time finger flexion task by attempting to flex fingers as though pressing a key on a keyboard.
source: On each trial, a letter appeared on the screen (e.g., 'T' for thumb). The participant was instructed to immediately flex the corresponding finger on the right hand (contralateral to the implant), as though pressing a key on a keyboard.
evidence: Description of the experimental task procedure.

claim: Participant NS's movement attempts did not generate overt motion due to her tetraplegia.
source: Because participant NS previously suffered a C3–C4 spinal cord injury resulting in tetraplegia (AIS-A), her movement attempts did not generate overt motion.
evidence: Direct statement about the lack of overt movement.

claim: Linear discriminant analysis with diagonal covariance matrices was used to classify finger movements from firing rate vectors.
source: To classify finger movements from firing rate vectors, we used linear discriminant analysis (LDA) with diagonal covariance matrices (Dudoit et al., 2002) (a form of regularization); diagonal LDA is also equivalent to Gaussian Naive Bayes (GNB) when GNB assumes that all classes share a covariance matrix.
evidence: Description of the classification method used.

claim: The able-bodied model RDM was generated using fMRI data from two independent studies with a total of 36 participants.
source: In Figure 2b, we generated an able-bodied model RDM using fMRI data from two independent studies, Kieliba et al., 2021 (N = 29, pre-intervention, right hand, 3T scans) and Ejaz et al., 2015 (N = 7, no intervention, right hand, 7T scans).
evidence: Description of the data sources used to construct the able-bodied model.

claim: The whitened unbiased RDM cosine similarity (WUC) metric was used to quantify model fit.
source: To quantify model fit, we used the whitened unbiased RDM cosine similarity (WUC) metric (Diedrichsen et al., 2021), which (Diedrichsen et al., 2021) recommend for models that predict continuous real values.
evidence: Description of the similarity metric used for model comparison.

claim: Participant NS's average PC-IP RDM was statistically typical when compared among individual able-bodied participants.
source: When compared among the RDM distribution of individual able-bodied participants, participant NS's average PC-IP RDM was statistically typical (permutation shuffle test, p = 0.55), in part because PC-IP fMRI RDMs were relatively variable across able-bodied participants (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison with able-bodied participant distribution.

claim: The 170 ms timing difference between muscle and somatotopy models roughly matches the delay between feedforward muscle activation and somatosensory afferents in able-bodied individuals.
source: The 170 ms timing difference we found roughly matches the delay between feedforward muscle activation and somatosensory afferents (Scott, 2016; Sollmann et al., 2017) in able-bodied individuals.
evidence: Comparison with known timing from literature on able-bodied individuals.

claim: PPC is thought to compute an internal forward model for sensorimotor control.
source: In this study, we recorded from the posterior parietal cortex (PPC), which is thought to compute an internal forward model for sensorimotor control (Mulliken et al., 2008; Wolpert et al., 1998; Desmurget and Grafton, 2000; Li et al., 2022).
evidence: Statement based on established scientific understanding from cited literature.

claim: A forward model overcomes inherent sensory delays to enable fast control by predicting upcoming states.
source: A forward-model overcomes inherent sensory delays to enable fast control by predicting the upcoming states.
evidence: Explanation of forward model function based on established neuroscience knowledge.

claim: In able-bodied individuals, cortical organization of finger representations follows the natural statistics of movements.
source: In able-bodied individuals, the cortical organization of finger representations follows the natural statistics of movements (Ejaz et al., 2015; Lillicrap and Scott, 2013).
evidence: Statement based on previous research findings.

claim: Visual occlusion in adult cats does not reorganize the visual cortex.
source: Visual occlusion in adult cats does not reorganize the visual cortex, and lesion studies of the adult visual cortex have arrived at competing conclusions of reorganization and stability (Smirnakis et al., 2005; Gilbert and Wiesel, 1992; Keck et al., 2008; Baseler et al., 2011).
evidence: Statement based on previous research findings in the literature.

claim: Classical studies posited that amputation and spinal cord injury modify the topography of body parts in S1.
source: Classical studies posited that amputation and spinal cord injury modify the topography of body parts in S1, with intact body parts taking over cortical areas originally dedicated to the amputated part (Merzenich et al., 1984; Qi et al., 2000; Pons et al., 1991; Jain et al., 2008).
evidence: Summary of classical findings from cited literature.

claim: Recent human neuroimaging studies and sensory BCI studies have challenged the extent of remapping, arguing that sensory topographies largely persist even after complete sensory loss.
source: However, recent human neuroimaging studies and sensory BCI studies have challenged the extent of this remapping, arguing that sensory topographies largely persist even after complete sensory loss (Makin and Bensmaia, 2017; Kikkert et al., 2021; Flesher et al., 2016; Armenta Salas et al., 2018).
evidence: Summary of recent findings from cited literature.

claim: Several paralyzed participants have been able to control BCI cursors by attempting arm or hand movements.
source: Several paralyzed participants have been able to control BCI cursors by attempting arm or hand movements (Hochberg et al., 2006; Hochberg et al., 2012; Collinger et al., 2013; Gilja et al., 2015; Bouton et al., 2016; Ajiboye et al., 2017; Brandman et al., 2018), hinting that motor representations could remain stable after paralysis.
evidence: Summary of findings from multiple BCI studies.

claim: Temporal dynamics provide another lens to investigate neural organization and its changes after paralysis.
source: Temporal dynamics provide another lens to investigate neural organization and its changes after paralysis.
evidence: Statement of the study's analytical approach.

claim: Motor cortex activity exhibits quasi-oscillatory dynamics during arm reaching.
source: Notably, motor cortex (MC) activity exhibits quasi-oscillatory dynamics during arm reaching (Churchland et al., 2012).
evidence: Statement based on previous research findings.

claim: Temporal structure can depend on the movement type and the recorded brain region.
source: More generally, the temporal structure can depend on the movement type (Suresh et al., 2020) and the recorded brain region (Schaffelhofer and Scherberger, 2016).
evidence: Statement based on previous research findings.

claim: PPC is thought to receive efference copies of motor command signals.
source: As such, PPC receives delayed multimodal sensory feedback and is hypothesized to receive efference copies of motor command signals (Mulliken et al., 2008; Andersen et al., 1997).
evidence: Statement based on hypotheses from cited literature.

claim: Because participant NS has no sensation below her shoulders, the somatotopy model is interpreted as the preserved prediction of sensory consequences of a finger movement.
source: However, because participant NS has no sensation below her shoulders, we interpret the somatotopy model as the preserved prediction of the sensory consequences of a finger movement.
evidence: Interpretation based on the participant's condition and observed neural dynamics.

claim: The sensory outcome signals could be the consequence of internal computations within the PPC or could come from other structures important for body-state estimation, such as the cerebellum.
source: These sensory outcome signals could be the consequence of internal computations within the PPC or could come from other structures important for body-state estimation, such as the cerebellum (McNamee and Wolpert, 2019).
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the source of sensory signals.

claim: Deafferentation appears to expand the remaining regions slightly, even while the pre-injury structure persists in the deafferented cortex.
source: Overall, deafferentation appears to expand the remaining regions slightly, even while the pre-injury structure persists in the deafferented cortex (Makin and Bensmaia, 2017).
evidence: Summary of findings from cited literature.

claim: Adult motor representations in PPC remain even after years without use.
source: Our results suggest that adult motor representations in PPC remain even after years without use.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the study's findings of preserved representations.

claim: The pre-injury properties of brain regions affect BCI performance.
source: However, our results and others (Smirnakis et al., 2005; Makin and Bensmaia, 2017; Kikkert et al., 2021; Hwang et al., 2013; Kikkert et al., 2016; Wesselink et al., 2019; Bruurmijn et al., 2017) suggest that the pre-injury properties of brain regions do affect BCI performance.
evidence: Inference drawn from the study's findings and cited literature.

claim: Representations may be remarkably persistent once formed.
source: Even though experience shapes neural organization (Merzenich et al., 1984; Ejaz et al., 2015; Wesselink et al., 2019), representations may be remarkably persistent once formed (Kikkert et al., 2021; Wesselink et al., 2019).
evidence: Inference drawn from the study's findings and cited literature.

claim: BCIs may benefit from tapping into the preserved, natural movement repertoire of motor areas.
source: Thus, even though BCIs bypass limbs and their biomechanical constraints (Lang and Schieber, 2004), BCIs may still benefit from tapping into the preserved, natural (Hwang et al., 2013) movement repertoire of motor areas.
evidence: Inference drawn from the study's findings about preserved representations.

claim: Participant NS could control the individual fingers of a virtual reality hand using the BCI.
source: These finger representations were robust across contexts and could be used in a range of environments, including to move the hand of a virtual reality avatar (Video 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by Video 1 showing virtual reality control.

claim: Participant NS was instructed to fixate on the target at least until the visual classification feedback was shown.
source: During both movement and No-Go trials, the participant was instructed to fixate on the target at least until the visual classification feedback was shown.
evidence: Description of the experimental task instructions.

claim: The classifier could not decode target location from neural activity during the attempted-movement period.
source: Furthermore, we could not decode the gaze location during the finger classification time window in the standard online-control task (Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: Supported by analysis showing inability to decode gaze location.

claim: Reliable finger representations emerged from the participant's movement attempts.
source: Thus, reliable finger representations emerged from the participant's movement attempts.
evidence: Inference drawn from control analyses ruling out visual confounds.

claim: The hand-usage model is nearly multicollinear with the muscle and somatotopy models.
source: Because the hand-usage model is nearly multicollinear with the muscle and somatotopy models (variance inflation factor: VIFusage,OLS = VIFusage,NNLS = 20.9, Methods), we first reduced the number of component models.
evidence: Supported by variance inflation factor analysis.

claim: The muscle + somatotopy model combination matched the data best.
source: Through a model selection procedure (Methods), we found that the hand usage + somatotopy and muscle + somatotopy model combinations matched the data best (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), with the muscle + somatotopy model matching the data marginally better.
evidence: Supported by model comparison analysis.

claim: Hand-usage and muscle activation patterns are strongly correlated for individual finger movements.
source: This ordering was consistent when exchanging the muscle and hand-usage component models (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 3), as hand-usage and muscle activation patterns are strongly correlated for individual finger movements (Overduin et al., 2012).
evidence: Statement based on previous research findings.

claim: The somatotopy model predicts that neighboring fingers will have similar cortical activity patterns.
source: The somatotopy model predicts that neighboring fingers will have similar cortical activity patterns (Ejaz et al., 2015), analogous to overlapping Gaussian receptive fields (Schellekens et al., 2018).
evidence: Description of the somatotopy model based on cited literature.

claim: The same PC-IP population encodes touch with Gaussian-like receptive fields.
source: In another study with participant NS, we found that the same PC-IP population encodes touch (Chivukula et al., 2021) with Gaussian-like receptive fields.
evidence: Reference to findings from another study with the same participant.

claim: Participant NS could use the BCI to acquire green jewels by pressing the corresponding finger in a virtual reality task.
source: She acquires green jewels by pressing the corresponding finger and avoids red amethysts by resting.
evidence: Description of the virtual reality task shown in Video 1.

claim: The study was approved by the California Institute of Technology, Casa Colina Hospital and Centers for Healthcare, and the University of California, Los Angeles Institutional Review Boards.
source: All procedures were approved by the California Institute of Technology, Casa Colina Hospital and Centers for Healthcare, and the University of California, Los Angeles Institutional Review Boards.
evidence: Statement of ethical approval for the study.

claim: Participant NS consented to the surgical procedure and subsequent clinical studies after understanding their nature, objectives, and potential risks.
source: She consented to the surgical procedure as well as to the subsequent clinical studies after understanding their nature, objectives, and potential risks.
evidence: Statement of informed consent.

claim: Neural signals were recorded, amplified, analog bandpass-filtered (0.3 Hz to 7.5 kHz), and digitized (30 kHz, 250 nV resolution).
source: Using the NeuroPort system (Blackrock Microsystems), neural signals were recorded from the electrode array, amplified, analog bandpass-filtered (0.3 Hz to 7.5 kHz), and digitized (30 kHz, 250 nV resolution).
evidence: Description of the neural recording methodology.

claim: Threshold crossings were detected at a threshold of −3.5× RMS.
source: Threshold crossings were detected at a threshold of −3.5× RMS (root-mean-square of an electrode's voltage time series).
evidence: Description of the spike detection methodology.

claim: K-medoids clustering was used to spike-sort the threshold crossing waveforms.
source: For all other analyses, we used k-medoids clustering on each electrode to spike-sort the threshold crossing waveforms.
evidence: Description of the spike-sorting methodology.

claim: The gap criteria were used to determine the number of waveform clusters for each electrode.
source: The gap criteria (Tibshirani et al., 2001) were used to determine the number of waveform clusters for each electrode.
evidence: Description of the clustering methodology.

claim: Experiments were conducted in 2–3 hr recording sessions at Casa Colina Hospital and Centers for Healthcare.
source: Experiments were conducted in 2–3 hr recording sessions at Casa Colina Hospital and Centers for Healthcare.
evidence: Description of the experimental setup.

claim: Participant NS viewed text cues on a 27-inch LCD monitor that occupied approximately 40 degrees of visual angle.
source: Participant NS viewed text cues on a 27-inch LCD monitor that occupied approximately 40 degrees of visual angle.
evidence: Description of the visual display setup.

claim: Cues were presented using the psychophysics toolbox for MATLAB.
source: Cues were presented using the psychophysics toolbox (Brainard, 1997) for MATLAB (Mathworks).
evidence: Description of the software used for stimulus presentation.

claim: The second experiment day was treated as two separate sessions due to a sizable rest period between morning and afternoon recordings.
source: The second experiment day (2018-09-17) was an exception, with data being recorded in a morning period and an afternoon period with a sizable rest in between. To reduce the effects of recording drift, we treated the two periods as separate sessions (i.e., spike-sorted each separately) for a total of 10 sessions.
evidence: Description of the session organization methodology.

claim: Each session consisted of a series of 2–3 min, uninterrupted 'runs' of the task.
source: Each session consisted of a series of 2–3 min, uninterrupted 'runs' of the task.
evidence: Description of the task structure.

claim: The condition order was block-randomized in the calibration task.
source: The condition order was block-randomized, such that each condition appeared once before repetition.
evidence: Description of the randomization procedure.

claim: Each screen in the primary task consisted of two repetitions each of T, I, M, R, P, and X arranged randomly on the grid.
source: Each screen consisted of two repetitions each of T (thumb), I (index), M (middle), R (ring), P (pinky/little), and X (No-Go) arranged randomly on the grid.
evidence: Description of the task design.

claim: Each trial in the primary task lasted 3 s.
source: Each trial lasted 3 s.
evidence: Description of the trial timing.

claim: Each cue was selected once (for a total of 12 trials) before the screen was updated to a new arrangement.
source: Each cue was selected once (for a total of 12 trials) before the screen was updated to a new arrangement.
evidence: Description of the trial structure.

claim: Each run consisted of three to four screens.
source: Each run consisted of three to four screens.
evidence: Description of the run structure.

claim: On each trial, 1.5 s after cue presentation, the classifier decoded the finger movement and presented its prediction via text feedback.
source: On each trial, 1.5 s after cue presentation, the classifier decoded the finger movement and presented its prediction via text feedback overlaid on the cue.
evidence: Description of the feedback timing and presentation.

claim: In the control task, the subject was instructed to saccade to each cued letter and fixate without attempting any finger movements.
source: The control task was similar to the primary task, except that the subject was instructed to saccade to each cued letter and fixate without attempting any finger movements.
evidence: Description of the control task procedure.

claim: No classification feedback was shown in the control task.
source: No classification feedback was shown.
evidence: Description of the control task procedure.

claim: Well-isolated single units were identified using the L-ratio metric.
source: Well-isolated single units were identified using the L-ratio metric (Schmitzer-Torbert et al., 2005).
evidence: Description of the unit quality assessment method.

claim: The neurons corresponding to the lowest third of L-ratio values were selected as 'well-isolated'.
source: The neurons corresponding to the lowest third of L-ratio values (across all sessions) were selected as 'well-isolated'.
evidence: Description of the unit selection criteria.

claim: A neuron was considered significantly tuned to a movement if p < 0.05 after FDR correction.
source: A neuron was considered significantly tuned to a movement if p < 0.05 (after FDR correction).
evidence: Description of the statistical significance threshold.

claim: Neurons with mean firing rates less than 0.1 Hz were excluded to minimize sensitivity to discrete spike counting.
source: Neurons with mean firing rates less than 0.1 Hz were excluded to minimize sensitivity to discrete spike counting.
evidence: Description of the neuron exclusion criteria.

claim: Input features for the BCI classifier were calculated by counting threshold crossings on each electrode during a 1-s time window.
source: Input features (firing rate vectors) were calculated by counting the number of threshold crossings on each electrode during a 1-s time window within each trial's movement execution phase.
evidence: Description of the feature extraction method.

claim: The exact time window for feature extraction was a hyperparameter for each session and was chosen to maximize cross-validated accuracy on the calibration dataset.
source: The exact time window was a hyperparameter for each session and was chosen to maximize the cross-validated accuracy on the calibration dataset.
evidence: Description of the hyperparameter optimization procedure.

claim: Electrodes with mean firing rates less than 1 Hz were excluded to prevent low-firing rate discretization effects.
source: To prevent low-firing rate discretization effects, we excluded electrodes with mean firing rates less than 1 Hz.
evidence: Description of the electrode exclusion criteria.

claim: During online control, the time window for feature extraction was fixed to [0.5, 1.5] s after cue presentation.
source: During online control of the finger flexion grid task, input features were similarly constructed by counting the threshold crossings from each electrode in a 1-s time window. This time window was fixed to [0.5, 1.5] s after cue presentation.
evidence: Description of the online control timing parameters.

claim: The window start time was chosen based on the estimated saccade latency in the first experimental session.
source: The window start time was chosen based on the estimated saccade latency in the first experimental session.
evidence: Description of the timing parameter selection rationale.

claim: The online classifier was occasionally retrained using data from the main task, usually every four run blocks.
source: The online classifier was occasionally retrained using data from this main task, usually every four run blocks.
evidence: Description of the classifier retraining procedure.

claim: Offline classification accuracy was computed using leave-one-out cross-validation within each session.
source: Offline classification accuracy (Figure 1—figure supplement 4) was computed using leave-one-out cross-validation (within each session).
evidence: Description of the offline analysis methodology.

claim: In the first session, the No-Go condition was not cued in the calibration task, so the classifier did not output No-Go predictions during that session.
source: In the first session (2018-09-10), the No-Go condition (X) was not cued in the calibration task, so the classifier did not output No-Go predictions during that session.
evidence: Description of a methodological detail specific to the first session.

claim: The cross-validated Mahalanobis distance measures the separability of multivariate patterns, analogous to LDA classification accuracy.
source: The cross-validated Mahalanobis distance, also referred to as the 'crossnobis' distance (Schütt et al., 2019), measures the separability of multivariate patterns, analogous to LDA classification accuracy (Nili et al., 2014).
evidence: Description of the distance metric properties.

claim: The fMRI ROI was selected to match participant NS's anatomical implant location (PC-IP).
source: The fMRI ROI was selected to match participant NS's anatomical implant location (PC-IP).
evidence: Description of the ROI selection procedure.

claim: RDMs were similar between the two fMRI studies' groups of participants based on a permutation shuffle test.
source: Based on a permutation shuffle test, RDMs were similar between the studies' groups of participants, so we aggregated the RDMs into a single dataset here.
evidence: Description of the data aggregation rationale.

claim: The hand-usage model was constructed using the velocity time series of each finger's MCP joint during everyday tasks.
source: The hand-usage model was constructed using the velocity time series of each finger's MCP joint during everyday tasks (Ingram et al., 2008).
evidence: Description of the hand-usage model construction.

claim: The muscle activity model was constructed using EMG activity during single- and multi-finger tasks.
source: The muscle activity model was constructed using EMG activity during single- and multi-finger tasks.
evidence: Description of the muscle model construction.

claim: The somatotopic model is based on a cortical sheet analogy and assumes that finger activation patterns are linearly spaced Gaussian kernels across the cortical sheet.
source: The somatotopic model is based on a cortical sheet analogy and assumes that finger activation patterns are linearly spaced Gaussian kernels across the cortical sheet.
evidence: Description of the somatotopic model construction.

claim: The rsatoolbox Python library was used to calculate data RDMs and compare them with model RDMs.
source: We used the rsatoolbox Python library (Schütt et al., 2019) to calculate data RDMs and compare them with model RDMs (RSA) (Kriegeskorte et al., 2008a).
evidence: Description of the software tools used.

claim: Pearson correlation assumes that observations are independent, but the elements of each RDM covary because the underlying dataset is shared.
source: Second, Pearson correlation assumes that observations are independent, but the elements of each RDM covary (Diedrichsen et al., 2021) because the underlying dataset is shared.
evidence: Explanation of the limitation of Pearson correlation for RDM comparison.

claim: WUC values should be interpreted by comparing against a baseline, usually chosen to be a null model where all conditions are pairwise-equidistant.
source: Thus, while correlation values can be compared against a null hypothesis of 0-correlation, WUC values should be interpreted by comparing against a baseline. The baseline is usually (Diedrichsen et al., 2021) chosen to be a null model where all conditions are pairwise-equidistant (and would thus correspond to 0-correlation).
evidence: Explanation of how to interpret WUC values.

claim: The noise ceiling estimates the maximum similarity possible given the observed variability between data RDMs.
source: To estimate the noise ceiling (Nili et al., 2014) (the maximum similarity possible given the observed variability between data RDMs), we assume that the unknown, perfect model resembles the average RDM.
evidence: Description of the noise ceiling calculation method.

claim: If a model achieves the noise ceiling, the model fits the data well.
source: If a model achieves the noise ceiling, the model fits the data well (Nili et al., 2014).
evidence: Explanation of the noise ceiling interpretation.

claim: Degrees-of-freedom for t-tests were conservatively estimated as the number of RDMs because individual elements of each RDM covary and are not independent.
source: For t-tests, we conservatively estimated the degrees-of-freedom as the number of RDMs, because the individual elements of each RDM covary and thus are not independent (Diedrichsen et al., 2021).
evidence: Description of the statistical analysis approach.

claim: Bayes factors were computed using the R package BayesFactor with default priors.
source: BFs were computed using the R package BayesFactor (Morey et al., 2015) with default priors.
evidence: Description of the Bayes factor calculation method.

claim: VIF values above 5 or 10 are common thresholds indicating that multicollinearity is a problem.
source: VIFOLS values above a threshold indicate that multicollinearity is a problem; VIF >5 or VIF >10 are common thresholds (James et al., 2013).
evidence: Statement of common statistical thresholds from cited literature.

claim: The 'one-standard error' rule was used to select the best parsimonious model.
